content: Single-shot spinal anaesthesia (SSS) and combined spinal-epidural (CSE) anaesthesia are both widely used techniques for providing anaesthesia during caesarean sections. Spinal anaesthesia is technically straightforward and provides a rapid onset of nerve blockade, but it is often associated with hypotension. In contrast, CSE anaesthesia allows for a more gradual onset of anaesthesia and the potential for prolonging the anaesthetic effect through the use of an epidural catheter. The objective of this review was to compare the effectiveness and adverse effects of CSE anaesthesia with single-shot spinal anaesthesia for caesarean sections. The review included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that compared these two techniques. Spinal anaesthesia was further categorised into high-dose (10 mg or more of bupivacaine) and low-dose (less than 10 mg of bupivacaine) subgroups. The review identified 18 trials involving 1272 women. However, most comparisons for individual outcomes included relatively small numbers of participants. The trials were conducted in various countries, including Australia, Croatia, India, Italy, Singapore, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, Turkey, the UK, and the USA. Overall, the trials were assessed as having a moderate risk of bias. CSE versus High-Dose Spinal Anaesthesia: There may be little or no difference between CSE and high-dose spinal anaesthesia in the number of women requiring a repeat regional block or general anaesthesia due to failure to establish adequate initial blockade. The evidence for this outcome is of low quality. It is uncertain whether there is any difference between the two techniques in the number of women requiring supplemental intra-operative analgesia or conversion to general anaesthesia during surgery. The evidence for these outcomes is of very low quality. The level of satisfaction with anaesthesia among women was also uncertain, with very low-quality evidence suggesting no clear difference between the two techniques. More women in the CSE group experienced intra-operative nausea or vomiting requiring treatment compared to the high-dose spinal group. There was no clear difference between the two groups in the incidence of post-dural puncture headache or intra-operative hypotension requiring treatment. None of the infants in either group had an Apgar score of less than seven at five minutes. CSE versus Low-Dose Spinal Anaesthesia: There may be little or no difference between CSE and low-dose spinal anaesthesia in the number of women requiring a repeat regional block or general anaesthesia due to failure to establish adequate initial blockade. The evidence for this outcome is of low quality. Similarly, there is probably little difference in the number of women requiring supplemental intra-operative analgesia. The evidence for this outcome is of moderate quality. The need for intra-operative conversion to general anaesthesia was not observed in any of the women in the trials, but the evidence for this outcome is of low quality. None of the studies assessed whether women were satisfied with their anaesthesia. The mean time to effective anaesthesia was faster in women who received low-dose spinal anaesthesia compared to CSE. However, the magnitude of this difference is unlikely to be clinically significant. CSE appeared to reduce the incidence of intra-operative hypotension requiring treatment compared to low-dose spinal anaesthesia. Similar numbers of women in both groups experienced intra-operative nausea or vomiting requiring treatment, and there were no cases of post-dural puncture headache. None of the infants in either group had an Apgar score of less than seven at five minutes. Authors' Conclusions: The number of studies and participants included in this review was small, and some of the trials had design limitations. There is some evidence suggesting that CSE may reduce the incidence of intra-operative hypotension compared to spinal anaesthesia, but it may also increase the likelihood of intra-operative nausea and vomiting requiring treatment. One small study found that low-dose spinal anaesthesia resulted in a faster time to effective anaesthesia compared to CSE, but the difference is unlikely to be clinically meaningful. Overall, there is insufficient evidence to support one technique over the other. Further high-quality, adequately powered studies are needed to evaluate the relative effectiveness and safety of CSE and spinal anaesthesia for caesarean sections. Future studies should also consider reporting economic aspects of these anaesthetic techniques.
